item.title: 3D Surface Matching Based on Adaptive Threshold and Curvature Map
item.description:
The problem

In industrial defect inspection and robotic sorting, 3D scanners have a limited acquisition range, so each scan yields a single point cloud or depth map taken from one viewpoint. This makes surface matching difficult: feature points are sparse, there is excessive redundant data, and the overlap rate is low.

How it works

The method matches a 3D workpiece model against a scene point cloud. It first reduces the model to its high-curvature feature domains, selected with an adaptive threshold, and then matches in two stages, coarse and fine.

  1. Depth and curvature maps. The model point cloud is converted into a depth map, and a surface curvature map is calculated from it.
  2. Adaptive threshold segmentation. An adaptive threshold iterative segmentation algorithm eliminates redundant points and retains the geometrically significant high-curvature feature points as the reduced model point cloud.
  3. Coarse matching. A coarse matching algorithm based on an integral volume descriptor identifies the approximate pose of the target point cloud within the scene point cloud, which the authors report improves coarse matching accuracy and robustness and reduces the dependence of ICP iterations on the initial pose.
  4. Fine matching. The iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm then achieves fine surface matching.

Results

Compared with conventional surface matching algorithms and manual threshold adjustment methods, the method achieves higher matching precision, aligning target workpieces accurately without misalignment or positional deviations.
In simulated low-to-medium noise environments it still matches correctly.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1109/ICIGP68997.2026.11619834.

item.title: Few-Shot 6D Object Pose Estimation via Decoupled Rotation and Translation with Viewpoint Encoding
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers an object’s 3D rotation and 3D translation relative to the camera, a core step for robotic grasping, autonomous driving and augmented reality. Depth sensors are affected by noise, occlusion and cost, and struggle with reflective or transparent objects, which motivates methods that use a single RGB image. Monocular methods based on keypoints, templates or direct regression have made steady progress, but they rely heavily on large annotated real datasets, and the scarcity of real pose annotations limits further gains.

This work decouples rotation from translation. Rotation is learned from synthetic images alone, so only the translation part is trained on real images, and the translation part does not have to learn rotation from them, which reduces the number of real samples needed.

How it works

An object detector first crops the object from the image. Rotation and translation are then estimated by two independent branches. The rotation branch factorises the full rotation R into an out-of-plane part Rγ (the object’s viewpoint) and an in-plane part Rθ (a rotation about the camera’s optical axis), R = RθRγ, and handles each with modules trained on synthetic images only. The translation branch builds on GDR-Net and is the only part trained on real images.

  1. Detect and crop. An object detector extracts a 128×128 region of interest (ROI) around the object from the RGB image; both branches work on this crop.
  2. Retrieve candidate viewpoints. A viewpoint encoder, trained on images rendered from ShapeNet, maps the ROI to a 64-dimensional vector that is sensitive to viewpoint but invariant to in-plane rotation. For the target object, 4,000 viewpoints are sampled uniformly on a sphere around its mesh and rendered to build a codebook; cosine similarity against the codebook gives the top-K candidate viewpoints.
  3. Regress the in-plane rotation. For each candidate, a regression head compares the ROI with the view rendered at that viewpoint and predicts the in-plane rotation, giving a complete 3D rotation hypothesis.
  4. Verify the orientation. A verification head scores how consistent each hypothesis is with the ROI, and the highest-scoring hypothesis is taken as the rotation estimate.
  5. Regress the translation. Following GDR-Net, a ResNet-34 predicts three 64×64 maps from the ROI (a dense 2D–3D correspondence map, a surface-region attention map and a visible-object mask), and a lightweight network regresses the scale-invariant translation from the correspondence and surface-region maps. This branch is trained with 600 real images per object.

Results

ADD(-S) is the share of poses with error below 10 % of the object’s diameter. 65.3 % ADD(-S) on LM-O, against 62.2 % for GDR-Net (Table 2).
65.9 % ADD(-S) and 92.4 % AUC of ADD-S on YCB-V, against 60.1 % and 91.6 % for GDR-Net (Table 4).
97.6 % ADD(-S) on LINEMOD with ground-truth ROIs, and 94.8 % with Fast R-CNN detections (Table 1).
Retrained with the same 600 real images, ZebraPose and CheckerPose reach 38.2 % and 40.5 % on LM-O, against 65.3 % here (Table 3).

The evaluation uses LINEMOD (13 objects in cluttered scenes), LM-O (8 partly occluded objects, 1,214 test images) and YCB-V (21 objects, with severe occlusion and several symmetric objects). A pose counts as correct when its ADD(-S) error is below 10 % of the object’s diameter; for YCB-V the area under the ADD(-S) curve up to 10 cm is reported as well. The rotation network is trained on synthetic images only and the translation network on 600 real images per object; for YCB-V, physically based rendered images are also used in training.

On LM-O the method is ahead of the compared methods on most objects, with the largest gains over GDR-Net on Holepuncher (74.5 % against 60.1 %), Duck and Ape; GDR-Net remains slightly better on Can and Eggbox. On YCB-V it also leads in AUC of ADD(-S), 86.9 % against 84.4 % for GDR-Net. The few-shot comparison shows the largest gap: when ZebraPose and CheckerPose are retrained with the same 600 real images, their YCB-V ADD(-S) falls to 35.7 % and 37.8 %, against 65.9 % here (Table 5). The rotation modules were also evaluated on their own on LINEMOD: on real images with predicted ROIs, viewpoint retrieval is within 10° in over 70 % of cases, and in-plane rotation is within 10° in 74 % of cases with predicted viewpoints and ROIs and in over 90 % with ground-truth viewpoints (Figs. 5 and 6), so in-plane accuracy depends strongly on retrieval quality. The authors note that accuracy partly depends on the reliability of the object detector, and that generalisation to unseen object categories remains limited.

item.title: Calibration Method of Fringe Projection Based on High-Order Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object, recovering the phase of the deformed fringes in the camera image, and converting pixel coordinates and phase into 3D coordinates. That conversion is set by system calibration, and the traditional approaches are laborious. Phase-to-height mapping needs a large, precise calibration target and a precision translation stage, and its parameters depend on how accurately both are made and moved. Stereo-vision calibration takes the target coordinates and their image coordinates in the camera and the projector, and solves for the parameters by nonlinear optimisation. That is slow, and the accuracy depends on how well those image coordinates are measured.

A polynomial calibration model avoids the projector model and the translation stage: it directly fits the 3D world coordinates as a polynomial in the pixel coordinates (u, v) and the absolute phase ϕ. Higher orders describe this relationship more accurately, but the number of coefficients grows quickly, and fitting them by least squares becomes slow and unstable once the order exceeds 3. An earlier simplification removes redundant terms by principal component analysis, which speeds the fit up but lowers reconstruction accuracy.

How it works

The method keeps a high-order polynomial calibration model, which needs no projector model and no translation stage, and replaces least-squares fitting with a sparse greedy randomized Kaczmarz (SGRK) solver. SGRK combines the efficient iterations of the randomized sparse Kaczmarz method with the selection strategy of greedy algorithms: each step works on one well-chosen equation instead of the whole system.

  1. Collect calibration points. Fringes are projected onto a circle-grid board placed in several poses. The circle centres are the feature points: each gives its pixel coordinates (u, v), its absolute phase ϕ from three-frequency four-step phase shifting, and its world coordinates from Zhang’s calibration method.
  2. Set up the polynomial model. Each world coordinate X, Y and Z is written as an n-th order polynomial in u, v and ϕ, so calibration becomes a linear system W = Ax. The model has 60 coefficients at order 3, 105 at order 4 and 168 at order 5; the paper uses order 4 as its standard model, balancing accuracy and computing time.
  3. Choose an equation greedily. In each iteration SGRK computes the residual of every equation, keeps the rows whose residual exceeds a threshold, and draws one of them with probability proportional to its squared residual. Equations with large errors are therefore updated first, which speeds up convergence.
  4. Update and sparsify. The chosen row updates the coefficients by a weighted Kaczmarz projection, and a soft-threshold operation then sets small coefficients to zero, so the solution stays sparse.
  5. Iterate, then reconstruct. The loop runs until the relative standard error (RSE) of the coefficients falls below 10⁻⁶. To measure an object, the pixel coordinates and absolute phase of each point are put into the fitted polynomial to give its 3D coordinates.

Results

Standard ceramic sphere (25.0001 mm), 4th-order model: diameter deviation 0.0232 mm in 1.63 s with SGRK, against 0.0727 mm in 3.96 s with least squares (Table 2).
Standard step block, 4th-order model: average errors of 0.004 and −0.003 mm on the two step heights in 1.78 s, against 0.009 and 0.006 mm in 4.32 s with least squares (Table 1).
Ceramic doll: RMSE 0.0729 mm with SGRK versus 0.9250 mm with least squares, measured against a Mech-Eye Pro S Enhanced scan (Sec. 3, Fig. 9).

The system uses a DLP LightCrafter 4500 projector (912 × 1140 pixels), a CCD camera (1280 × 1024 pixels) and a 300 mm × 300 mm circle board with 30 mm between circle centres. Each method was compared on the full 4th-order model and on the PCA-simplified 4th-order model. SGRK was faster and more accurate in both cases: on the sphere the simplified model gave 0.0449 mm in 1.17 s with SGRK against 0.0932 mm in 3.17 s with least squares, and the simplified models were less accurate than the full one for both solvers (Table 2). The step block was measured three times after each calibration to check repeatability (Table 1).

The advantage holds at other orders too (Table 3). At order 3, SGRK gave a sphere diameter deviation of 0.0549 mm in 1.02 s against 0.1470 mm in 3.04 s for least squares; at order 5, 0.0177 mm in 2.31 s against 0.0400 mm in 6.15 s. The 5th-order model is more accurate than the 4th, but its 168 coefficients make the computation markedly longer, and both are more accurate than the 3rd-order model.

item.title: WTAYOLO: A Detection Model for Weak Scratches on Metal Surfaces
item.description:
The problem

Scratches on the surface of lithium batteries significantly affect their electrochemical performance and operational safety, so stringent scratch detection is crucial for product quality. Detection remains difficult, however: lithium battery materials are reflective, and the morphology of the scratches themselves makes them hard for detection algorithms to pick up.

How it works

WTAYOLO is a detection model for weak scratches on metal surfaces. It combines photometric stereo imaging, which tackles the reflections, with a new module, WTAConv, which improves how scratch features are extracted from the images.

  1. Photometric stereo imaging. WTAYOLO uses a photometric stereo system, which reduces interference from surface reflections.
  2. A wider receptive field. The WTAConv module expands the receptive field, strengthening the extraction of scratch features from the images.
  3. Channel and spatial attention. Within WTAConv, channel and spatial attention mechanisms strengthen important features and suppress redundant information.
  4. Scratch detection. The model detects the subtle scratches.

Results

mAP50 of 86.8 %, a 5.1 % improvement over the YOLOv11n baseline, without increasing the number of parameters.

The authors conclude that the method strikes an effective balance between accuracy and model cost-effectiveness, providing an effective solution for industrial applications.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1145/3725949.3725956.

item.title: High-precision three-dimensional data real-time progressive rendering method and system
item.description:
This patent addresses real-time visualization of high-precision 3D data. Progressive rendering lets large point clouds or dense 3D measurement results become interactive before the full dataset is loaded or drawn at maximum detail.

This work appears in CN Patent WO2022257594A1(PCT).

Algorithm principle

The method organizes 3D data for progressive display, allowing coarse visual feedback first and higher-detail rendering as more data becomes available. This is useful when industrial 3D scans are too large for immediate full-resolution interaction.

Visual material

Detailed method and result figures will be added when the patent assets are available.

Results and impact

The patent supports the visualization side of industrial 3D inspection, where users need to inspect dense geometry without long waiting times.

item.title: Sequencing in Transformation of Rasterized 3D Models
item.description:
The problem

A rasterized 3D structure is built from discrete, equal-sized parts, the way a picture is built from pixels: voxels in a computer, and cubes, bricks or food cans in the physical world. Such parts are easy to process as data, easy to reuse and suited to mass production. The thesis asks how to change one such structure into another. It frames this as a transformation from a source structure to a destination structure, and looks for an efficient sequence of operations that a machine can follow, with efficiency measured by an application-dependent cost function. Building a structure from a material palette is a special case, in which the source is the palette.

The difficulty is that the problem is discrete. Even deciding which part goes where is a combinatorial problem: for n parts there are n! possible assignments. The lowest-cost assignment is not necessarily executable either. A suction gripper can only pick parts on the top surface, a LEGO brick cannot be picked while other bricks cover or surround it, and a brick cannot be placed where it would hang in the air. Sequencing therefore has to trade the total amount of work against physical feasibility, and for bricks also against how many of the source parts are reused.

How it works

The thesis studies three cases that, in its words, represent the majority of sequencing problems for transforming and shaping rasterized structures: pick-and-place of homogeneous voxels (Chapter 3), pick-and-place of heterogeneous LEGO bricks (Chapter 4), and folding of voxel chains (Chapter 5). The explainer follows the thesis’s worked voxel example step by step, then places the other two cases alongside it.

  1. Align and classify. Both mesh models are rasterized into voxels. Assuming they are already aligned vertically and only translation is allowed, an exhaustive search in the horizontal plane finds the alignment with the largest overlap. Voxels present only in the source are movers (M), voxels present only in the destination are voids (V), and overlapped voxels stay where they are. If the numbers of M and V differ, the extra voxels go to, or come from, a linear stack.

  2. Price every move. The cost function models a three-axis Cartesian machine that moves sideways only at a clearance plane zmax: the cost cij of moving mover i into void j is cij = |xj − xi| + |yj − yi| + 2zmax − zi − zj. Pairing every M with a V at minimum total cost is an assignment problem, which the Hungarian method solves in O(n3) time instead of comparing n! options.

  3. Respect top access. With a vacuum suction gripper, only voxels on the top surface can be picked or placed. Pairing all M and V at once (the global optimisation strategy, GOS) gives a lower bound on the cost, but the pairs may deadlock. The local optimisation strategy (LOS) builds the cost matrix only from the M and V that are currently accessible, applies the Hungarian method, and moves those pairs.

  4. Update and repeat. After each round the top surfaces change, a new cost matrix is built, and the process repeats until every M has been placed. In the worked example LOS reaches a total cost of 27, the same as the GOS lower bound. Two simpler baselines are also compared: a greedy strategy (GSS) that moves only the single cheapest accessible pair at each step, and a random one (RSS).

  5. Extend to bricks and chains. Bricks (LEGO). Voxels are merged into bricks layer by layer. The rigid approach (RT) generates both brick layouts before transformation, and the flexible approach (FT) generates the target layout on the fly, preferring brick types that are movable on the source. Each approach is combined with three strategies for routing bricks through a buffer and a stock (see the figure below), giving six algorithms, RT1–RT3 and FT1–FT3, named after the approach and the strategy number.

    The algorithms are scored by cost (the number of pick-and-place actions), reuse rate (the share of source bricks that end up in the target) and an overall performance that grows with reuse and falls with cost.

    Chains. A shape is turned into a 1D string by finding a Hamiltonian path through its voxels. The path is made possible either by pruning and appending voxels or by dividing each voxel into 4 (2D) or 8 (3D) sub-voxels. The fold is then planned from the difference between the start and target joint angles.

Results

LOS near the GOS lower bound, in seconds instead of over an hour: for wall → pyramid (1,643 M-V pairs), LOS costs 60,199 against the GOS lower bound of 60,021, and computes in 9.5 s against 4,440 s (Table 3.1).
LEGO reuse against cost: in the Growlithe → Charmander transformation with colour information, FT3 reuses 56.1% of the source bricks with 3,203 pick-and-place actions, while FT1 reuses 69.3% with 6,015 (Test 3, Fig. 4.13).
FT3 has the best overall performance averaged over 56 transformations at each of seven model sizes; RT2 is the best of the rigid algorithms (Fig. 4.9).

The voxel strategies were tested on eight models (wall, pyramid, starfish, cube, igloo, castle, stairs and the Eiger mountain), each rasterized to between 2,250 and 2,550 voxels and transformed into every other. GOS always gives the lowest cost but does not by itself define a feasible sequence, and it is the slowest, because it runs the Hungarian method once on a very large cost matrix. LOS is second in cost, GSS slightly worse, and RSS clearly worse but fastest. The work is set by the number of M-V pairs, not by model size: wall → pyramid needs 1,643 pairs, while the more similar pyramid → igloo needs only 325. Across rasterization resolutions, the total cost grows about linearly with the number of pairs, and so does the time of LOS, even though the Hungarian method itself is O(n3). LOS stands out for the balance it strikes between cost and computation time. Its stated limitation is the top-access constraint, which rules out overhanging structures. Bricks that lock together, like LEGO, can form overhangs, which motivates the LEGO chapter.

For LEGO, eight triangle-mesh models were converted to brick models. In the average over all pairwise transformations, cost rises linearly with model size, and Strategies 1, 2 and 3 cost successively less. Strategies 1 and 2 reach very similar reuse rates, so the thesis concludes that disassembling the whole source up front is not worthwhile. FT reuses more bricks than RT, but its bricks tend to be smaller than the best fit, which gives weaker structures with internal sliding planes and more bricks in the target. FT3 reaches a reuse rate comparable to the best RT algorithms, and in the transformations from one model to the other seven it matches the reuse of FT1 and FT2 at a much lower cost. With colour information (114 colours, and exterior bricks must match in colour as well as shape), reuse falls but does not drop to zero, because interior bricks may take any colour. The thesis notes that the overall-performance metric is empirical, and that the relative ranking may change in scenarios that define cost differently.

Two directions are left as future work: adding force analysis such as finite element analysis, so that intermediate structures as well as the final one are stable, and transforming at the level of modules (groups of parts moved as a whole) rather than single parts, which the thesis expects to improve both reuse rate and cost.
